SK1094 Use nullable reference type syntax instead of an annotation attribute

A JetBrains.Annotations [CanBeNull] or [NotNull] states in an attribute what the nullable context can state in the type.

CategoryModernization
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floorC# 8.0
Since2.0

Why

⚠ This rule exists because of the retirement. A codebase leaving ReSharper is a codebase that has to drop its JetBrains.Annotations dependency, and every [CanBeNull] in it is a nullability fact that either moves into ? or is lost — silently, because the attribute stops meaning anything the moment nothing reads it. No other tool reports these, and after the switch-off nothing will. The compiler's own annotation is also strictly stronger: it is checked at every call site rather than by a tool the build does not run.

Example

Instead of:

[CanBeNull]
public string Name { get; set; }

Write:

public string? Name { get; set; }

When it does not fire

⚠ The nullable annotation context is read at the declaration, not from the project. In a #nullable disable file the attribute is the only nullability signal there is, and rewriting T to T? there produces CS8632 and loses the fact — so the rule withdraws whenever the annotation context at the site is off, whichever way the compilation-level default is set. ⚠ `JetBrains.Annotations` only. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis attributes are deliberately untouched: [MaybeNull] T Get<T>() on an unconstrained T says something T? genuinely cannot, which is the reason that attribute exists, and a rule that did not know the difference would delete the annotation and the meaning with it. Only reference types are reported for the same reason — an unconstrained type parameter is not one, so it is never matched. ⚠ `[NotNull]` on a type already written `T?` is declined. The attribute and the syntax disagree, the repair depends on which of them the author meant, and guessing wrong writes the opposite contract. The three cases that are reported are unambiguous: [CanBeNull] on T becomes T? with the attribute removed, and [CanBeNull] on T? or [NotNull] on T is an attribute restating what the type already says, so only the attribute goes. A declaration carrying both attributes is declined outright rather than reported twice with overlapping edits. ⚠ fixIsSafe is false, against the proposal, and the measurement is the reason: annotating a parameter or a field T? is a contract change, and it surfaces the CS8602s that the attribute had been describing all along. Those warnings are the migration doing its job, not the fix misfiring, but they are exactly what fixIsSafe: true promises will not appear — so the rule asks to be reviewed rather than lying about it.
